- Your filesystem is damaged
- A scheduled job is deleting the files (check the modification time of the directory to see when the deletion happens)
- A file sync program (like Dropbox) is getting confused and removing the files
- If you're browsing to the files from Finder, the files may have some attribute set that makes them hidden (but I think they should still be visible from the command line)

messages.subject: Food for thought from an interactive NYT graphic
messages.subject_clean: Food for thought from an interactive NYT graphic
messages.body_plain:
I just saw this cool map showing the development of Manhattan's grid:
http://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2011/03/21/nyregion/map-of-how-manhattan-grid-grew.html

They did some interesting things that would be cool to have in some future version of ggplot. Even if it's not possible to implement them, I think it's useful to consider how various graphics could be described with the grammar of graphics.

First off, the map is interactive -- you can zoom and pan. This is sort of like using coord_cartesian and setting its parameters interactively with a mouse.

With the Street Openings overlay, there's a slider that lets you control what time-slice of the data is shown. It would be really nice to be able to specify a mapping like "slider=year", or something like that. With the Growth overlay, there are four different years that are clickable; you click on a year to see the census data from that year. Conceptually, these things let you interactively view a subset of the data. As far as I can tell, interactivity is something that can't be described very well with aesthetic mappings or with faceting.

Even the 1811 and 1836 overlay maps could be implemented with something this, using a geom_raster for the overlay map. However, instead of mapping a data value to the slider, you'd map alpha to the slider.

There are many practical issues with doing this, such as:
- Grid graphics doesn't have sliders or other interactive components (as far as I know)
- Most export formats don't support interaction (though maybe PDF does?)

Even so, it would be nice if the data structures in the new layers package could support interactive data presentation, even if the present rendering backend doesn't.

Thoughts?

messages.body_plain:
I think that the pieces already exist in various places, but the
question is how to coordinate them all in ggplot2. The NYT plot to
which you refer appears to be an example of a 'Hans Rosling plot',
basically a set of static plots of the same phenomenon with the same
x-y axis limits done over time and strung together with a slider. The
googleVis package provides one way to make these sorts of plots in R.

Two packages that seem relevant to this enterprise are animation and
RGoogleMaps. The NYT plot is done in GoogleVis, but I can't tell if
it's through R or not. In the googleVis package, you arrange the data
to make a call to googleVis, which then renders the (animated)
graphic. See the googleVis demo for some examples; the googleVis
package description provides a few more links. Michael Friendly did a
couple of googleVis plots in the Lahman package (see the examples
under the hitters data).

googleVis is self-contained - you feed the data and the plot call
function from the package and R communicates with the GoogleVis
application to produce the graphic. To do something similar with
ggplot2, one option would be to create a series of static plots and
then use the animate package to string them into a video display. I
seem to recall that a few people have used ggplot2 in conjunction with
RGoogleMaps to produce some neat displays, so perhaps some combination
of ggplot2, RGoogleMaps and animation would provide parallel
functionality to googleVis for graphs similar to the one referenced
here.

Heike Hoffman did some animation for the airlines data:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Flying-over-the-usa
so this sort of thing has been done before with ggplot2, but I don't
think it's been systematized yet. See also
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Crime-in-Downtown-Houston%2C-Texas-%3A-Combining-ggplot2-and-Google-Maps
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Using-ggplot2-animations-to-demonstrate-several-parallel-numerical-experiments-in-a-single-layout

The use of sliders to handle time and zooming is another issue that
probably requires some means of adding interactivity to the package
and that's likely to be a nontrivial concern. I'll bet it's on
Hadley's long term radar screen, though, so I'm looking forward to his
take on this, as well as that of others.

Dennis

> > are common in all geoms,

> > lineend = "butt", linejoin = "round", linemitre = 1), na.rm = FALSE)

> > for decoration.
>
> Hmmmmmmm, I'm not sure I see a big advantage in doing it this way.
> Most geoms will have few additional parameters, and making decoration
> a separate list makes it a pain to (e.g.) set lineend = "round"
> without setting the other decorations.

This talk of decorations is related to something that's been on my mind for a while...

I'll start by talking about existing issues with mapping vs. setting aesthetics. One of the things that ggplot2 beginners have the hardest time with is the distinction between putting a variable inside of aes() as opposed to outside of it. I can understand the confusion -- I remember experiencing it myself at one point.

Adding to the confusion is that variables that are set (outside of aes) get mixed in with other stuff. Here's an example:
  geom_bar(aes(fill=var1), colour="black", position="dodge")
In this case, 'colour' is similar to 'fill' in that it's an aesthetic, but syntax-wise, it's on a par with 'position', which is something else entirely. It does all makes some sense after you've been using it a while and internalize the concept of aesthetics and mappings, but at first this can be challenging.

One possible solution is to make it so users have to be more explicit about what's mapped and what's set, as in:
  geom_bar(aes(fill=var1), set(colour="black"), position="dodge")

In other words, all mapped vars go in aes(), all the set variables go in set(), and other stuff goes outside. The trade-off for the added clarity is a little verbosity, but I think it's worth it -- I think it'll both be easier for beginners to understand, and force them to start thinking the right way.

I don't know if what I've laid out above is the best way to do it... Maybe stat parameters should be separated too. To transition the system to this syntax, it might make sense to still accept the previous syntax but throw warnings about deprecated behavior.

Moving on to "decoration"... These could be treated as aesthetics that can only be set; mapping variables to them is invalid. Conceptually speaking, decorations are aesthetic properties -- just ones that it doesn't make sense to map variables to. Here's an example where 'linejoin' is the decoration:
  geom_bar (aes(fill=var1), set(colour="black", linejoin="round"))

If someone tries to map a variable to 'linejoin', then it could just give an error about it not being a mappable aesthetic.

>From a development point of view, one advantage of doing things this way is that you could implement something as a decoration at first, and then later you could promote it to a mappable aesthetic, without breaking existing user code. For example, maybe today I think that 'arrow' should be a decoration (can set, but not map), but for the next version of ggplot2, I decide that it should be a mappable aesthetic. It would be possible to add this capability without interfering with existing user code.

Overall, I think main the advantages to doing this way are conceptual clarity and syntactic consistency, and the drawback is slightly more verbose syntax.

-Winston

I agree that geom_bar is currently quite confusing - it mixes
parameters for the layer, the geom and the stat (but not the
adjustment!).  In the future, I'd like to geom_bar to refer
specifically to the geom (as it does in the layers package).  There
it's quite clear what arguments geom_bar has:

geom_bar <- function(aesthetics = list(), na.rm = FALSE) {
  ...
}

i.e. a list of aesthetics and a parameter controlling what happens to missing.

So the first thing I'd like to do when clearing up the general
parameter confusion is to clear up the confusion between the geom and
the layer.

In the future, to add a "bar chart" layer to a plot, you'd use
layer_bar.  I think this would look like:

layer_bar <- function(mapping, data, geom = "bar", stat = "identity",
adjust = "stack", inherit.aes = TRUE, show_guide = NA) {
  ..
}

which would be shortcut for

layer_bar <- function(mapping, data, geom = geom_bar(), stat =
stat_identity(), adjust = adjust_stack(), inherit.aes = TRUE,
show_guide = NA) {
  ..
}

The most explicit way of specifying (e.g.) blue bars would be:

layer_bar(geom = geom_bar(list(fill = "blue")))

The challenge is coming up with a short cut form that works in most
situations.  One option would be to adapt what happens currently (but
with a better design for stats, geoms and adjusts this code would be
simpler and more flexible).  For example, just focussing on the geom
part:

layer_bar <- function(geom = "bar", ...) {
  args <- list()
  if (is.character(geom)) {
    geom <- match.fun(paste("geom", "bar", sep = "_"))
    geom_args <- args[intersect(names(args), names(formals(geom)))]
    geom <- geom(geom_args)
 }
 stopifnot(is.geom(geom))
 ...
}

So then you could do:

layer_bar(aesthetics = list(fill = "blue"))

I'm still thinking about the names of the arguments and their order,

If you're serious about being able to export, I'd like to suggest a way of thinking about this. Instead of thinking about exporting the data for d3, we should consider providing a platform-agnostic description of the graph.

Here's the question to consider: What information is necessary to fully describe the desired output?  I think this should be the output of ggplot2_build, or some other function in the pipeline. This description could then be translated and rendered with a grid-based rendering system, as is currently done, or gridSVG, or even d3.

In order to answer the question, we need to specify the baseline capabilities of all drawing platforms that will be used to render the grpah (e.g., grid, gridSVG, and d3). Right now, ggplot2 is built around grid graphics. This means if the output of ggplot2_build() refers to grid-specific aesthetics like size, shape, and linetype, it can't be used by another drawing platform like d3, without hacking in how 'linetype' works in grid.

The procedure might be something like this:
1. start with data + ggplot specification
2. use ggplot_build to generate platform-agnostic description of the graph (call it the PAD)
3. give the description to a drawing platform (e.g., a grid-based system or d3)

Each drawing platform may have capabilities beyond the baseline. For example, it looks like gridSVG's capabilities are a superset of grid's, and d3's capabilities may overlap with grid without being a super- or subset. And grid itself may have more capabilities than the baseline.

You could also allow use of extended capabilities of each drawing platform. For example, imagine that gridSVG supported a slider control. You could then give a PAD with sliders to a gridSVG-based platform and it would come out fine. But if you gave the same PAD to a grid-based platform, it would throw a warning or error.

If things all worked out this way, the PAD could used as a standard data interchange format -- it could be generated by something other than ggplot2 in R, and rendered by something other than ggplot2 in R.

All of that said, I realize that it may be totally impractical to completely abstract away from the individual drawing platforms. And there's a danger of going too far and building an entire graphics system when the payoff isn't large enough to warrant it. But, at the very least, this could be a useful tool for thinking about how to structure things.

Also, I agree that having real examples with d3 is a good idea, since it's always helpful to have something concrete to look at.

-Winston

This is a really weird problem, and I'm not sure what's causing it.
Function arguments should be evaluated in the environment in which
they are created.  It's possible the problem occurs because [ is a
primitive function and so behaves a little different.

The fix is to force the evaluation of range before it gets passed to [

discard <- function(x, range = c(0, 1)) {
  force(x)

  x[x >= range[1] & x <= range[2]]
}

and similar for all the other bounds function.  I'm starting teaching
today, so I don't have time to fix it right now, but a patch to scales
would be appreciated, or I'll try to get to it later in the week.

Hadley

Hi,

Skimming through the latticeExtra webpage, I found this idea (among
others) quite interesting to share:

http://latticeextra.r-forge.r-project.org/#panel.key&theme=theEconomist

Squeezing the legend inside the plot panel is something that's often
needed for journals with tight length limits. Having a convenient
interface to specify the position of the legend inside a panel would
be quite useful. Currently, opts(legend.position) is given in
normalised units relative to the full ggplot viewport, which requires
trial and error in my experience (and ggplot2 can be slow..)

If the legend grob can be extracted, or perhaps even only a part of it
(e.g. only linetype goes to one panel), some variation of
annotation_custom() could be used to place it inside one panel, with a
position given as data coordinates (including Inf for convenience),
and the standard justification hjust,vjust.

Best,

baptiste

Quite possibly, yes. However, the idea of making it an annotation
instead is that ggplot2, in its logic, would always by default use an
external location for the legend (which always works, for all plots),
but for the final cosmetic tweaks before publication one could
disassemble the plot and place the legend in a very plot-specific
position. In this regard, having it as an annotation also gives more
freedom to modify the grob with grid before placing it, or even use a
different grob altogether (a feature that should probably not be
implemented in the pure grammar of graphics framework where the legend
should be purely automated, but could be useful as a kind of
post-processing -- an annotation).

messages.subject: Passing models to geom_smooth
messages.subject_clean: Passing models to geom_smooth
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

A recent discussion on the main ggplot2 list spurred me on to try to make it possible to pass a model object to geom_smooth/stat_smooth.

I made some changes to make it possible to use the syntax geom_smooth(model=mymodel), where mymodel is a model object. The change was fairly trivial -- you can see it here:
https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/commit/6f6c34cbaea46071bca0ae9da3c18585c871fa89

It doesn't make use of fortify, which was one possibility that was discussed. Instead, it uses the predictdf functions in stat-smooth-methods.r.

Right now it works with a single predictor. But it doesn't work if you have multiple predictors, which you might want with color mappings or facets. I have a feeling that getting multiple predictors to work will require much more extensive changes.

You can try it out by installing my experimental branch:
install_github("ggplot2", "wch", "experimental")

Here are some examples:

set.seed(123)
x <- runif(20, 0, 10)
z <- factor(rep(c("foo", "bar"), each=10))
y <- x*(0.5*as.numeric(z)) + (3+as.numeric(z)) + runif(20, 0, 3)
dat <- data.frame(x, y, z)

# Works
modlm <- lm(y ~ x, data = dat)
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(model = modlm)

# Works
modloess <- loess(y ~ x, data = dat)
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(model = modloess)

# Doesn't work: 2 variables
modlm2 <- lm(y ~ x + z + x:z, data = dat)
ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + facet_wrap( ~ z) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(model = modlm2)

-Winston

Greetings:

Attached is a first draft of what is intended to be a transition guide
for ggplot2 users moving from 0.8.9 to 0.9.0. I'd like to ask you to
look it over and provide feedback to me about things that are missing
or could be improved either in the examples or text. Most of the new
geoms are illustrated  as well as the guide functions, but I'm sure
I'm missing things that could improve the document in a number of
ways. Organizational tips are welcome, too. The goal is to try to get
the average user of ggplot2 up to speed more quickly with respect to
the current changes and additions in the package.

I've deliberately omitted providing examples of the new stat_
functions, but it would be useful to include more examples where the
code in 0.8.9 does not work in 0.9.0 and what the replacement code
would be. I envisioned that as a separate section of the document, to
be 'rbinded' to the current version.

This document was produced with the new knitr package developed by
Yihui Xie from Iowa State. I thank him for his help on the several
occasions I've bothered him today about different aspects of the code.
If you like what you see, install the package from CRAN and go to its
website to learn more about it: http://yihui.github.com/knitr/

Several plots in this document were changed from pdf to png to reduce
the file size; if you print this and find a few of the graphs rather
grainy or pixillated, that's why. There are also three places in the
document where bugs in the current 0.9.0 are pointed out; I know that
two of them are reported and I'm sending a message about the third one
this evening just in case. Since bugs are usually fixed pretty
quickly, hopefully the correct output will be there soon.

Also note that this is a transition guide for experienced users of
ggplot2 and not an introductory tutorial. Feel free to reply through
the list or privately.

Dennis

On Sun, Jan 22, 2012 at 3:43 PM, Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com> wrote:

> This is completely different in a way but Does relate to graphing model objects.  I think it would be nice if there could be other RHS variables.  Thus for example you could have a scatter plot for x and y with one line showing the effect of x on y; and a second showing the conditional effect of x on with w and z in the model.  Equivalent to:
>
> y ~ x
> y ~ x + w + z
>
> To use predict() this would require the creation of a new data frame where x was the same but w and z were held at their mean/median or for factors, perhaps mode or the referent group based on contrasts.  In the past, I have done all of this outside ggplot2 and ten just passed a final data frame with c and expected y values to geom_line() but if work is being done with stat_smooth that would allow models, perhaps it could also allow selection of hitch aspects of the model to plot and what values to hold the other terms at.
>

Now that I've thought about this a bit more, I've realized that this whole thing may need more consideration about how it should work... The way things currently operate, if your data is grouped (say, with color, or facets) and you add a geom_smooth() to it, it makes a model for each individual group, independent of each other. This is different from passing in a single model that contains these variables.

Here's an example that will illustrate.

dat <- data.frame(
        x = c(0,10,0,10,0,10),
        y = c(0,10,10,0,5,5),
        z = c(1,1,2,2,3,3))

# Get lm
mod <- lm(y ~ x + z + x:z, data=dat)
fortify(mod)
#  y  x z      .hat   .sigma .cooksd .fitted .resid .stdresid
#  0  0 1 0.8333333 6.123724   1.250     2.5   -2.5        -1
# 10 10 1 0.8333333 6.123724   1.250     7.5    2.5         1
# 10  0 2 0.3333333 6.123724   0.125     5.0    5.0         1
#  0 10 2 0.3333333 6.123724   0.125     5.0   -5.0        -1
#  5  0 3 0.8333333 6.123724   1.250     7.5   -2.5        -1
#  5 10 3 0.8333333 6.123724   1.250     2.5    2.5         1

ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(method=lm) +
    geom_line(aes(y=.fitted), colour="red", data=mod) +
    facet_grid(. ~ factor(z))

The blue lines are the result of stat_smooth, where each facet gets its own linear model. The red lines are the result of a linear model y ~ x + z + x:z. As you can see, the lines are different. This itself is not a problem, but it does show that passing in a single model is different from using stat_smooth.

Here are the two cases spelled out:
1. A model is built for each group. (This is what stat_smooth does.)
2. A single model is used across all groups. (This is done in the example above with the geom_line.)

I wanted to allow syntax like this:
  mod <- lm(y ~ x+z+x:z, data=dat)
  ggplot(dat, aes(x,y)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(model=mod) +
    facet_grid(. ~ factor(z))
... but I don't think this syntax is expressive enough to handle case (1), since it just passes in one object.

My original goal was to make it possible to have access to the model objects _and_ to easily plot the model objects with ggplot2. Presently, in case (1), it's easy to plot the models, but not to have access to the objects. In case (2), it's possible to plot the objects with the geom_line thing I used above (which internally makes use of fortify), and also have access to the model objects. But if you do it this way, the interface is not particularly clear and there's not a simple way to get confidence regions. Also, there presently are not S3 methods for fortify for many other types of model objects besides lm -- there's no fortify.glm or fortify.loess, for example.

At any rate, what would be nice is a simple, consistent interface to plot and get the model objects in cases (1) and (2). If anyone has thoughts about what such an interface interface would look like, please feel free to share.

-Winston

This itself is not a problem, but it does show that passing in a single model is different from using stat_smooth.

That's because the behaviour of lm is different depending wether the explanatory variables are numeric or factors. When an explanatory variable is numeric, then it just uses that as an additional predictor (think of it as y = a.x1 + b.x2 + c instead of just y = a.x + b , in pseudo mathematical terms). When an explanatory variable is a factor, it splits the regression per level. Either the intercepts are different, or the slope is different, or both.

In you example above, the difference comes from the fact that z is a factor for ggplot (hence the ability to split) and not for the regression. With this:

    dat <- data.frame(
            x = c(0,10,0,10,0,10),
            y = c(0,10,10,0,5,5),
            z = c(1,1,2,2,3,3))

    dat$z <- factor(dat$z)

    mod <- lm(y ~ x + z + x:z, data=dat)

    ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(method=lm) +

        geom_line(aes(y=.fitted), colour="red", data=mod) +
        facet_grid(. ~ factor(z))

the two approaches are indeed identical.

You can check this further in a less caricatural case this way:

	library("plyr")
	set.seed(123)
	dat <- data.frame(x=runif(20), y=rnorm(20), z=factor(rep(c(1,2), each=10)))

	# fit a model per level, separately
	ddply(dat, ~z, function(X) {
		lm(y ~ x, data=X)$coefficients
	})

	# fit a model per level, with one call
	lm(y ~ x + z + x:z, data=dat)$coefficients

In that case, z=1 is taken as the reference level and the coefficient z2 is the difference in intercept between z=1 and z=2, and x:z2 is the difference in slope between z=1 and z=2. You could also write it this way

	lm(y ~ z + x:z, data=dat)$coefficients

in which case the slopes (z1:x and z2:x) will be computed independently and not with one as the difference from the other (and you would find exactly what you get from the separate models). But the first syntax is the usual ANCOVA approach (because the test for the second slope has H0 = differences of slope = 0, and it therefore tells you wether you need to actually consider a separate slope model or wether the same slope can be used across levels).

And, you probably guessed it, but to get the same intercept but a different slope you do

	lm(y ~ x + x:z, data=dat)

while to get the same slope but a different intercept

	lm(y ~ x + z, data=dat)

I hope this clears things a little.

Of course for the representation, things get tricky when you get two (or more) numeric predictors: the regression is not a line anymore relative to anyone of those two, it is a plane in the y,x,z space (where y is the response and x and z two numeric explanatory variables). I've been looking for a good way to represent the results of multivariate regressions or a while. In the general case (n explanatory variables, n>2), I can't find one. Suggestions are welcome ! ;)

wanted to pass along a work around I found for (what I consider to be) a
deficiency GitHub: given an already existing Issue (say a bug report
someone has submitted) and a subsequently written patch on someone's

attached to that issue.  A pull request results in a new issue (though
possibly with a reference if it contains something like "fixes #xx" in
the commit message).  Here is discussion of a workaround using git at
the command line:

I suppose I should say I have not tried either the "hub" or command line
git method, but they look promising.

If this is useful to anyone, please use it; if not, ignore it.

On Mon, Jan 23, 2012 at 5:15 PM, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:

> > That's because the behaviour of lm is different depending wether the explanatory variables are numeric or factors. When an explanatory variable is numeric, then it just uses that as an additional predictor (think of it as y = a.x1 + b.x2 + c instead of just y = a.x + b , in pseudo mathematical terms). When an explanatory variable is a factor, it splits the regression per level. Either the intercepts are different, or the slope is different, or both.
> >
> > In you example above, the difference comes from the fact that z is a factor for ggplot (hence the ability to split) and not for the regression. With this:
> >
> >    dat <- data.frame(
> >            x = c(0,10,0,10,0,10),
> >            y = c(0,10,10,0,5,5),
> >            z = c(1,1,2,2,3,3))
> >
> >    dat$z <- factor(dat$z)
> >
> >    mod <- lm(y ~ x + z + x:z, data=dat)
> >
> >    ggplot(dat, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(method=lm) +
> >        geom_line(aes(y=.fitted), colour="red", data=mod) +
> >        facet_grid(. ~ factor(z))
> >
> > the two approaches are indeed identical.
>
> That's a slight simplification - they're very close, but not
> identical.  The difference is that if you fit the models separately
> each model has a different estimate for the overall standard error.

Well, I took another stab at it and managed to solve the variable name issue. It now passes the model object to fortify() to get predicted values. I was only able to test it with lm, since fortify.xx isn't defined for very many other classes, and I'm not familiar with the ones that it is defined for.

If versions of fortify.xx are written for other types of models, I think they should work with this code, as long as the returned data frame contains a column .fitted with predicted values at each x.

A few other notes:
- There presently is no provision for including confidence regions, since that information isn't provided by fortify.lm. But if standard errors were also by fortify, it should be possible to do confidence regions. This would result in some duplication of functionality between fortify.xx and predictdf.xx in stat-smooth-methods.r. If development continue in this direction, it would probably be a good idea to look into unifying them somehow.

- Right now it will get confused if there are predictors in the model that aren't "used up" by the x axis plus the other aesthetics/facets. (e.g., if you use mod2 below without facets)

- Because it needs to access the variables in the data frame before they're renamed to x, y, colour, etc., the code must be put in the user-facing function geom_smooth, rather than the proto object GeomSmooth (because GeomSmooth is later in the pipeline and only sees the remapped data). This is definitely unusual, and hopefully won't require too much hackiness down the road.

If you want to see the code, here's the commit: https://github.com/wch/ggplot2/commit/d9578e
It can be installed using my experimental branch:

  install_github("ggplot2", "wch", "experimental")

Here are some examples, with the results attached. The shaded regions are from the stat_smooth's calculations, not from the model that's passed in manually.

set.seed(111)
dat <- data.frame(
       wvar = rep(c(1,2,3), each=3),
       xvar = rep(c(0,5,10), 3),
       yvar = c(0,5,10, 10,5,0, 5,5,5) )

# Treat wvar as a factor for lm
dat$wvar <- factor(dat$wvar)

# Add a little noise to yvar
dat$yvar <- dat$yvar + runif(9)

# Using one predictor
# Blue line and shaded region is from stat_smooth(method=lm)
# Red dashed line is from passing in model
mod1 <- lm(yvar ~ xvar, data=dat)
ggplot(dat, aes(x=xvar, y=yvar)) + geom_point() +
  stat_smooth(method=lm) +
  geom_smooth(model=mod1, colour="red", linetype="dashed", size=1.5)

# Using two predictors, faceted on factor w
mod2 <- lm(yvar ~ xvar + wvar + xvar:wvar, data=dat)
ggplot(dat, aes(x=xvar, y=yvar)) + geom_point() +
  stat_smooth(method=lm) +
  geom_smooth(model=mod2, colour="red", linetype="dashed", size=1.5) +
  facet_grid(. ~ wvar)

-Winston

To give my opinion on a few of the open questions:

- how to return things when a data.frame is not enough? This is the case for PCA where you typically have the coordinates of the objects and the coordinates of the variables. I decided, in concert with Hadley to use a named list of data.frames. It seems like the only logical solution in this case. Putting everything in a single data.frame does not make sense and there's not one data.frame that's more relevant than the other so putting one of the two as attribute would be meaningless. I feel that the list would be the best solution in most cases.

- names and methods: the package name will be autoplot and all fortify and autoplot methods will be exported (to make it easy to look at the code, which is essential if you want to tweak the plot further)

- extends vs depends: in the case of the special package with only fortify/autoplot methods, it will depend on ggplot. In the case of a few methods defined for special object in the specialized package, I would lean towards extends/recommends ggplot rather than explicitly depend on it, since it is likely than default plot methods will also exist.

`autoplot` should define default aesthetic mappings but allow the user to override them. One way to do it is to have a `mapping` argument to autoplot and then define the actual mapping as:

If you're talking about moving the code I added to the new package, you might want to wait a bit, because I realized that there's probably a better way to do it. It also presently doesn't interpolate (it only gets values at the x values in the original data), so if your model is supposed to have a curve, it will end up looking like a bunch of straight line segments.

> The only conceptual issue that I could see with this is that fortify should, in essence, be a way to *extract* information from the model object and that SE is not explicitly computed in the model object.

My view is that this isn't really a problem. The various models I've worked with seem to be inconsistent in the information they provide, and in the way the information is structured.

One concern I have is that if the SE values from predict() are used to draw confidence regions, those confidence regions might be misleading when using a single model and splitting it up on a factor. In this example, using the same data as before, the confidence regions from the single model (red) are much narrower than the confidence regions from the three separate models generated by stat_smooth (gray).

set.seed(111)
dat <- data.frame(
       wvar = rep(c(1,2,3), each=3),
       xvar = rep(c(0,5,10), 3),
       yvar = c(0,5,10, 10,5,0, 5,5,5) )

# Treat wvar as a factor for lm
dat$wvar <- factor(dat$wvar)
# Add a little noise to yvar
dat$yvar <- dat$yvar + runif(9)

mod2 <- lm(yvar ~ xvar + wvar + xvar:wvar, data=dat)

mod2pred <- cbind(mod2$mode, predict(mod2, se=TRUE, interval="confidence")$fit)

ggplot(dat, aes(x=xvar, y=yvar)) + geom_point() +
  stat_smooth(method=lm) +

  geom_line(data=mod2pred, aes(y=fit), colour="red", linetype="dashed") +
  geom_ribbon(data=mod2pred, aes(ymin=lwr, ymax=upr), fill="red", alpha=.2) +
  facet_grid(. ~ wvar)

This is the difference that Hadley mentioned. I don't know that one way is right and the other is wrong, but it would be good to make sure people know what they're getting into. (Obviously, if SE's and confidence intervals aren't provided by fortify or plotted, then this isn't an issue.)

I had been checking the main CRAN page for ggplot2 to see when the
windows build was available, and saw the regression to 0.8.9. Now I know
why.  Additional comments inline below.

On 1/27/2012 7:53 AM, Winston Chang wrote:
> That's really unfortunate. I wonder if this means that it will be
> impossible to change the public API of a package once it other packages
> become dependent on it.
>
> I also wonder how the changes should be synchronized. Say that a dependent
> package uses ggplot2 in one way, but the new version of ggplot2 is changed
> to do it another way, which breaks the dependent package. Then which
> package do you change first in CRAN? Either way it would lead to a bad
> build.
>
> Maybe it's possible to semi-support old behavior but throw warnings about
> deprecated behavior. I'd guess that some of these breakages are due to the
> use of scale_x_log2 and scale_x_log, which no longer exist in 0.9.0. Maybe
> if ggplot had those functions, but just threw warnings about deprecated
> behavior -- or messages, if warnings break the build of dependent packages.

Using deprecation to phase out behavior is the way to do this.
Effectively, you go through the entire interface (all exported
functions, all of their arguments) [side note: another reason to keep
the number of exported functions as small as possible; partly why I
don't like too many "helper" functions] and make sure that the new
version supports all the functions/arguments. However, for those that
you want to replace, you add a warning() saying that it is deprecated
and will be removed in a future version.  A later version can then
change the warning to a stop(), and a version after that can change the
function signature to no longer support the interface.  This allows a
transition phase where in the beginning, other code will work but will
produce warnings which can prompt the code to be updated.  This would
also have the effect of showing good-faith efforts to get dependent
packages up-to-date rather than suddenly breaking.

Yes, this is more work, but can be aided by the testing to make sure
that warnings (and later errors) are thrown at the right time/right
combination. Basically, planned obsolescence, with warning.

Here is an example:

In ggplot2 0.8.9, the signature for scale_x_continuous is

function (name = NULL, limits = NULL, breaks = NULL, labels = NULL,
     trans = NULL, expand = c(0.05, 0), minor_breaks = NULL, formatter =
"scientific",
     legend = TRUE, ...)

where ... is ignored.

In ggplot2 0.9.0, the signature for scale_x_continuous is

function (..., expand = c(0.05, 0))

where ... is "common continuous scale parameters: name, breaks, labels,
na.value, limits and trans. See continuous_scale for more details" and
continuous_scale lists names, breaks, minor_breaks, labels, legend,
limits, rescaler, oob, na.value, and trans; aesthetics, scale_name,
palette, and guide are set by the function call itself (and can not be
overridden).  Looking at these sets, the only one not supported is
formatter.

Since scale_x_continuous is basically a wrapper anyway,
scale_x_continuous can be changed to:

scale_x_continuous <- function(..., expand = c(0.05, 0), formatter) {
   if (!missing(formatter)) {
     warning("formatter argument to scale_x_continuous is deprecated.
Formatting of scale labels now handled by providing a function to the
label argument. formatter argument ignored.")
   }
   continuous_scale(c("x", "xmin", "xmax", "xend", "xintercept"),
"position_c", identity,
     ..., expand = expand, guide = "none")
}

What you do with it can vary:
* State it is deprecated, at minimum
* Include hint as to what functionality replaces it (even better with
reference to appropriate help page)
* If feasible, map the old functionality to the new. Here, I didn't
bother to even try. Some places it will be easy, some it will be
impossible. If not, stating that the argument is ignored is good

Doing this, things break "softly." They still run, but may give warnings
and may not be exactly what it was in the past.  But it also has hints
to what should be done to upgrade it.

This is also testable.

test_that("scale_x_continuous deprecated formatter", {
   expect_warning(scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent"))
})

Here is how it looks in action:

qplot(x=runif(40), y=sample(40)) +
   scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent")

 > qplot(x=runif(40), y=sample(40)) +
+   scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent")
Warning message:
In scale_x_continuous(formatter = "percent") :
   formatter argument to scale_x_continuous is deprecated. Formatting of
scale labels now handled by providing a function to the label argument.
formatter argument ignored.

But a plot is made.  Not identical to what you get in 0.8.9, but it
doesn't break.  Without this, you get

 > qplot(x=runif(40), y=sample(40)) +
+   scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent")
Error in continuous_scale(c("x", "xmin", "xmax", "xend", "xintercept"),  :
   unused argument(s) (formatter = "percent")

Functions that were removed get re-stubbed, again with a warning.

scale_x_log1p <- function(...) {
   warning("scale_x_log1p is deprecated. Use
scale_x_continuous(trans=log1p_trans()) where log1p_trans is in the
scales package")
   scale_x_continuous(..., trans=log1p_trans())
}

 > qplot(x=rexp(40,0.001), y=sample(40)) +
+   scale_x_log1p()
Warning message:
In scale_x_log1p() :
   scale_x_log1p is deprecated. Use
scale_x_continuous(trans=log1p_trans()) where log1p_trans is in the
scales package

These could all be put in a single deprecated stubs file.

At some future version, warning can be changed to stop and bridging code
can be removed (and expect_warning changed to expect_error).  At a
version after that, the signature can be altered and the checks removed
entirely (whether tests remain is optional); anything that would break
should already have broken by then.  If it has not been fixed at that
point, it's not going to be. But the authors have been given plenty of
chance to fix it.

If this is is the approach to take, here is something to help get started.

(in a session with ggplot2 0.8.9):

gg089funs <- ls("package:ggplot2")
names(gg089funs) <- gg089funs
gg089args <- llply(gg089funs, function(f) {names(formals(get(f)))})
#save(gg089funs, gg089args, file="gg089.RData")

(in a session with ggplot2 0.9.0):

gg090funs <- ls("package:ggplot2")
names(gg090funs) <- gg090funs
gg090args <- llply(gg090funs, function(f) {names(formals(get(f)))})
#load("gg089.RData")

missingfuns <- setdiff(gg089funs, gg090funs)
commonfuns <- intersect(gg089funs, gg090funs)
diffargs <- list()
for (fun in commonfuns) {
   dff <- setdiff(gg089args[[fun]], gg090args[[fun]])
   if (length(dff) != 0) {
     diffargs[[fun]] <- dff
   }
}

Dear all,

Apologies for breaking your code with the recent ggplot2 package. I
think the best solution for now is to withdrawal ggplot 0.9.0 from
CRAN. I'll re-upload it on March 1 giving everyone some time to
respond to the changes.

If you'd like to try out your package with the development version of
ggplot2, the easiest way is to use devtools:

install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("ggplot2")

If you'd like help figuring what breaks, please join the ggplot2
development mailing list (http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2-dev),
and we'll help you out, either by providing a fix to your code, or by
fixing the underlying problem in ggplot2.

Sorry for not anticipating this problem - I didn't realise how much
ggplot2 had grown in popularity since the last time I released a new
version.

Hadley

>
> Hadley
>
>

>
> I am really sorry that my update to ggplot2 has broken your previously

> resources to ensure that every version of ggplot2 is perfectly
> backward compatible with the previous version (even if I did have the

> broken because a package can  not depend on a specific version of
> another package, only on the most recent version.  This is the root of
> the problem, and means the only way I can add new features/fix bad

>
> Hadley
